Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Assertiveness: never disagree or assert myself to avoid conflict, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Hopelessness: I have no future, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Twenty years ago, Dennis, a 66-year-old Southeast Asian American, was working late on a commercial flat roof when a ruptured tank of industrial sealant released a heavy plume of volatile fumes. The sky had darkened, and his headlamps flickered out, leaving him standing in shadow while the air grew thick and burning. He tried to step back, but his lungs seized. He woke hours later in a hospital bed, where the sharp, clinical antiseptic scent clung to the walls and his wife’s coat. What stayed with him was the unblinking clarity of that moment: the exact angle of his boots slipping on the wet membrane, the suffocating heat in his chest, the way the chemical smoke swirled against the streetlights. Over the following weeks, those memories began to play in his mind like a reel of film that refused to stop, each loop just as detailed as the last. Sometimes, without any picture at all, the old panic would simply crash over him, as if his body were still breathing that air. The symptoms accumulated slowly, beginning as an inability to relax even in his own bed. His wife would wake to find him sitting upright, shoulders tight, convinced he could not afford to let his guard down. The world had become a place where danger waited around every corner, and he could no longer trust himself to judge a situation or react quickly enough. He began avoiding unfamiliar places altogether, unable to map out escape routes before entering a room. Work demanded a parallel vigilance. While re-roofing a commercial warehouse last November, the sudden drop into darkness triggered a cold knot in his stomach. He would pace the ridge, scanning for leaks that weren’t there, waiting for the light to return. At job sites using industrial adhesives, a whiff of something chemical would send his heart hammering, forcing him to step away and breathe through the sudden tightness. To manage the distress, Dennis built quiet routines around his life. He stopped disagreeing, even when his crew foremen questioned his choices, because conflict felt too destabilizing to navigate. He drilled his mind away from the exposure the moment a memory tried to surface. Yet the trauma persisted alongside his daily routines. He found himself sitting on the porch in the evenings, lost in what he used to be like before the chemicals. He told himself he had no future, that his ability to rely on himself had been permanently fractured. Concentration frayed during his day, his attention drifting off the ridge or the spreadsheets he used to track invoices, leaving him to double-check finished measurements. For months, these habits narrowed his world until his life fit entirely within familiar streets and job sites. What finally brought him to the clinic was the slow erosion of his marriage and his trade. His wife noticed how he flinched at the hospital’s cleaning supplies during her follow-up appointment, and how he now turned down contracts requiring unfamiliar industrial parks. He had come to believe that stepping into the unknown was a gamble he could no longer afford. In his first session, Dennis sat with his hands folded tightly in his lap, his voice steady but edged with exhaustion. He did not know if the old certainty could return, or if he had to learn to live with a mind that kept replaying the exposure on a loop. He wanted to stop bracing for a collapse that never came, and he hoped someone could help him find a way to trust the ground beneath his boots again.
